claim: The brainstem plays a crucial role in sleep-wake regulation.
source: The brainstem plays a crucial role in sleep-wake regulation.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the manuscript's focus and cited literature on brainstem involvement in sleep-wake cycles.

claim: Brainstem populations can predict pupil dilation and vigilance states on a timescale of seconds to minutes.
source: On a timescale of seconds to minutes, brainstem populations can predict pupil dilation and vigilance states and exhibit longer prediction power than hippocampal CA1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4, showing predictive relationships between brainstem neural activity and pupil diameter/behavioral states.

claim: Brainstem populations exhibit longer prediction power for vigilance states than hippocampal CA1 neurons.
source: On a timescale of seconds to minutes, brainstem populations can predict pupil dilation and vigilance states and exhibit longer prediction power than hippocampal CA1 neurons.
evidence: This is directly supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 4C, where brainstem and hippocampal CA1 decoding performances are compared.

claim: Pontine waves (P-waves) are accompanied by synchronous firing of brainstem neurons during both REM and NREM sleep.
source: On a timescale of sub-seconds, pontine waves (P-waves) are accompanied by synchronous firing of brainstem neurons during both rapid eye movement (REM) and non-REM (NREM) sleep.
evidence: This is supported by the peri-event time histograms in Figures 5G and 5H showing coordinated firing of brainstem neurons around P-wave timing.

claim: During NREM sleep, hippocampal sharp wave-ripples (SWRs) precede P-waves.
source: Crucially, P-waves functionally interact with CA1 activity in a state-dependent manner: during NREM sleep, hippocampal sharp wave-ripples (SWRs) precede P-waves.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the temporal analysis in Figure 7D showing that SWRs occur before P-waves during NREM sleep.

claim: P-waves during REM sleep are phase-locked with ongoing theta oscillations.
source: On the other hand, P-waves during REM sleep are phase-locked with ongoing theta oscillations and are followed by burst firing of CA1 neurons.
evidence: This is supported by phase analysis shown in Figures 6 and 7, demonstrating significant phase-locking between P-waves and theta oscillations during REM sleep.

claim: P-waves during REM sleep are followed by burst firing of CA1 neurons.
source: On the other hand, P-waves during REM sleep are phase-locked with ongoing theta oscillations and are followed by burst firing of CA1 neurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C, where peri-event time histograms demonstrate CA1 neural firing following P-waves during REM sleep.

claim: Sleep states are typically classified into two major states: non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and REM sleep.
source: Sleep states are typically classified into two major states, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and REM sleep.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about sleep classification.

claim: Numerous brain regions and cell-types have been identified as part of sleep-regulating circuits.
source: While numerous brain regions and cell-types have been identified as part of sleep-regulating circuits (Brown et al., 2012; Héricé et al., 2019; Jouvet, 1962; Moruzzi, 1963; Peever and Fuller, 2017; Scammell et al., 2017; Weber and Dan, 2016; Luppi et al., 2017; Adamantidis et al., 2007; Tsunematsu et al., 2014; Weber et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2019), sleep-related neural firing and oscillations have also been described across cortical and subcortical regions (McCarley and Hobson, 1971; Hobson et al., 1975; Sakai, 1985; Steriade, 2006; Brown et al., 2012; Rasch and Born, 2013; Buzsáki, 2015; Weber et al., 2015; Scammell et al., 2017; Weber et al., 2018; Héricé et al., 2019; Liu and Dan, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to prior literature.

claim: Cortical slow oscillations, sleep spindles and hippocampal sharp wave-ripples (SWRs) are prominent neural events during NREM sleep.
source: For example, cortical slow oscillations, sleep spindles and hippocampal sharp wave-ripples (SWRs) are prominent neural events during NREM sleep, whereas theta oscillations and ponto-geniculo-occipital (PGO) or pontine (P) waves are seen during REM sleep (Steriade, 2006; Montgomery et al., 2008; Buzsáki, 2015; Buzsáki, 2002; Jouvet, 1969; Steriade et al., 1993b; Callaway et al., 1987; Datta, 1997; Rasch and Born, 2013; Bizzi and Brooks, 1963).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on sleep-related neural oscillations.

claim: Theta oscillations and ponto-geniculo-occipital (PGO) or pontine (P) waves are seen during REM sleep.
source: For example, cortical slow oscillations, sleep spindles and hippocampal sharp wave-ripples (SWRs) are prominent neural events during NREM sleep, whereas theta oscillations and ponto-geniculo-occipital (PGO) or pontine (P) waves are seen during REM sleep (Steriade, 2006; Montgomery et al., 2008; Buzsáki, 2015; Buzsáki, 2002; Jouvet, 1969; Steriade et al., 1993b; Callaway et al., 1987; Datta, 1997; Rasch and Born, 2013; Bizzi and Brooks, 1963).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on REM sleep neural events.

claim: Little is known about population activity within the brainstem.
source: Although neural ensemble dynamics underlying these sleep-related neural events in the thalamus and the cortex including the hippocampus have been well described (Steriade, 2006; Buzsáki, 2015; Buzsáki, 2002; Steriade et al., 1993a), little is known about population activity within the brainstem.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: The brainstem, including the midbrain, pons and medulla has long been implicated in the sleep-wake cycle.
source: The brainstem, including the midbrain, pons and medulla has long been implicated in the sleep-wake cycle (Jouvet, 1962; Saper et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2012; Rasch and Born, 2013; Weber et al., 2015; Weber and Dan, 2016; Luppi et al., 2017; Scammell et al., 2017; Héricé et al., 2019; Liu and Dan, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior research on brainstem involvement in sleep-wake regulation.

claim: The brainstem contains various nuclei, each of which consists of diverse cell-types and exhibits state-dependent firing.
source: It contains various nuclei, each of which consists of diverse cell-types and exhibits state-dependent firing (Brown et al., 2012; Rasch and Born, 2013; Weber et al., 2015; Weber and Dan, 2016; Luppi et al., 2017; Scammell et al., 2017; Héricé et al., 2019; Liu and Dan, 2019; Weber et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on brainstem anatomy and function.

claim: Recorded regions spanned across multiple nuclei, including the sublaterodorsal nucleus, pontine reticular nucleus, medial preoptic nucleus, parabrachial nucleus, pontine central gray, laterodorsal tegmental nucleus and other surrounding areas.
source: Recorded regions spanned across multiple nuclei, including the sublaterodorsal nucleus, pontine reticular nucleus, medial preoptic nucleus, parabrachial nucleus, pontine central gray, laterodorsal tegmental nucleus and other surrounding areas according to post-mortem histological analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on histological verification of recording sites shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wakefulness was characterized by high muscle tone and pupil dilation.
source: wakefulness was characterized by high muscle tone (Figure 1D) and pupil dilation (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figures 1D and 1F.

claim: NREM sleep was characterized by higher power of slow oscillations and a wider dynamic range of pupil diameter.
source: whereas NREM sleep was characterized by higher power of slow oscillations (Figure 1C) and a wider dynamic range of pupil diameter (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figures 1C and 1F.

claim: REM sleep was distinct from the other states, with respect to prominent theta oscillations, low muscle tone, higher brainstem LFPs power and fully constricted pupil.
source: REM sleep was distinct from the other states, with respect to prominent theta oscillations (Figure 1C), low muscle tone (Figure 1D), higher brainstem LFPs power (Figure 1E) and fully constricted pupil (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figures 1C-F.

claim: The higher power of brainstem LFPs during REM sleep was preserved across all animals (seven animals, nine recordings).
source: The higher power of brainstem LFPs during REM sleep was preserved across all animals (seven animals, nine recordings) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The sleep architecture, cortical EEGs and EMGs were generally comparable between head-fixed and tethered unfixed conditions.
source: Although most of our recordings were performed under a head-fixed condition, the sleep architecture, cortical EEGs and EMGs were generally comparable with those in a tethered unfixed condition (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Four functional classes of brainstem neurons were identified: awake (AW)-on neurons (23.7%), REM-off neurons (17.1%), REM/AW-on neurons (6.6%), and REM-on neurons (52.6%).
source: We identified four functional classes: awake (AW)-on neurons (23.7%) were more active during wakefulness than during sleep states; REM-off neurons (17.1%) reduced their firing during REM sleep; REM/AW-on neurons (6.6%) were quiet during NREM sleep; and the largest class (52.6%) was REM-on neurons, which showed the highest firing rate during REM sleep.
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis of state-dependent firing rates shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cholinergic populations showed larger activity during REM sleep and wakefulness than during NREM sleep (F2,32 = 5.12, p=0.012, one-way ANOVA).
source: Consistent with the data from in vivo electrophysiology, cholinergic populations showed larger activity during REM sleep and wakefulness than during NREM sleep (F2,32 = 5.12, p=0.012, one-way ANOVA) (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fiber photometry data shown in Figures 2E-G with statistical analysis.

claim: Pupil diameter is an excellent biomarker of global brain state or arousal level.
source: Pupil diameter is an excellent biomarker of global brain state or arousal level (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Yüzgeç et al., 2018; Larsen and Waters, 2018; McGinley et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on pupil diameter as a biomarker.

claim: Activity in brainstem neurons, especially in locus coeruleus norepinephrine neurons, correlates with pupil diameter.
source: and activity in brainstem neurons, especially in locus coeruleus norepinephrine neurons, correlates with pupil diameter (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The effects of behavioral states on pupil diameter was statistically significant (F2, 53 = 220.33, p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA).
source: The effects of behavioral states on pupil diameter was statistically significant (Figure 3A, F2, 53 = 220.33, p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA), with pupil diameter being constricted during REM sleep and dilated during wakefulness.
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of pupil diameter data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Pupil diameter was constricted during REM sleep and dilated during wakefulness.
source: The effects of behavioral states on pupil diameter was statistically significant (Figure 3A, F2, 53 = 220.33, p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA), with pupil diameter being constricted during REM sleep and dilated during wakefulness.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Pupil diameter dynamically fluctuated during wakefulness and gradually constricted during NREM sleep.
source: With respect to pupil dilation dynamics across states (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), pupil diameter dynamically fluctuated during wakefulness and gradually constricted during NREM sleep.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 10–20 s before REM sleep, the pupil diameter would further decrease and was fully constricted during REM sleep.
source: Typically, 10–20 s before REM sleep, the pupil diameter would further decrease and was fully constricted during REM sleep (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most of the neurons showed asymmetric profiles of R2 values when predicting pupil dilation.
source: As expected, most of the neurons showed asymmetric profiles of R2 values (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the linear regression analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The average profile showed brainstem neuron activities that were predictive of pupil diameter around 10 s in advance.
source: Although individual profiles were diverse, the average profile showed brainstem neuron activities that were predictive of pupil diameter around 10 s in advance.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of R2 values shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Changes in brainstem neural activity preceded those in pupil diameter.
source: Thus, changes in brainstem neural activity preceded those in pupil diameter.
evidence: This is inferred from the asymmetric predictability profiles shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Brainstem populations have predictive power for pupil diameter.
source: Thereby, brainstem populations have predictive power for pupil diameter.
evidence: This is concluded from the multiple linear regression analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) is a technique that finds compact and easily interpretable representations of neural population activity in the form of parts-based activity patterns.
source: To address this, first, we extracted the features of neural population activity by applying non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), a technique that finds compact and easily interpretable representations of neural population activity in the form of parts-based activity patterns (Lee and Seung, 1999; Onken et al., 2016) (Figure 4A and B) (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on NMF methodology.

claim: NMF was able to extract several modules that captured state-dependent firing patterns across neurons in an unsupervised fashion.
source: Overall firing rate reflected state changes (Figure 4A), whereas NMF was able to extract several modules that captured state-dependent firing patterns across neurons in an unsupervised fashion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the NMF analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Module 1 represented REM-on activity, whereas module 2 was activated at the end of NREM sleep and module 3 was most active during wakefulness.
source: For example, module 1 represented REM-on activity, whereas module 2 was activated at the end of NREM sleep and module 3 was most active during wakefulness.
evidence: This is based on the NMF analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The weights in each module were consistent with the state-dependency of individual neural firing.
source: Indeed, the weights in each module were consistent with the state-dependency of individual neural firing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Brainstem populations showed predictive activity tens of seconds before transitions into all three behavioral states.
source: Brainstem populations showed predictive activity tens of seconds before transitions into all three behavioral states.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the decoding analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hippocampal neurons are well known to exhibit state-dependent firing.
source: Of many brain regions, hippocampal neurons are well known to exhibit state-dependent firing (Buzsáki, 2002; Buzsáki, 2015; Mizuseki and Miyawaki, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on hippocampal neural activity.

claim: CA1 neurons also had predictive power for several tens of seconds, but the profile was relatively short-lasting compared to that of brainstem neurons.
source: Although CA1 neurons also had predictive power for several tens of seconds, the profile was relatively short-lasting compared to that of brainstem neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Brainstem neurons have longer-lasting predictive power for behavioral states than hippocampal CA1 neurons.
source: Thus, brainstem neurons have longer-lasting predictive power for behavioral states than hippocampal CA1 neurons.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: P-waves appeared more often during REM sleep (p<0.0001, two-tailed t-test).
source: These neural events appeared more often during REM sleep (p<0.0001, two-tailed t-test) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The frequency of P-waves gradually increased during NREM to REM sleep transitions and decreased during REM sleep to wakefulness transitions.
source: Intriguingly, the frequency of these events gradually increased during NREM to REM sleep transitions and decreased during REM sleep to wakefulness transitions (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the temporal evolution analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: These neural events are P-waves in mice.
source: Because these characteristics generally resemble those in other species (Callaway et al., 1987; Datta, 1997), we concluded that these neural events are P-waves in mice.
evidence: This conclusion is based on comparison with characteristics of P-waves in other species, supported by citations.

claim: Many of the simultaneously recorded brainstem neurons fired during P-waves.
source: Many of the simultaneously recorded brainstem neurons fired during P-waves.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the example shown in Figure 5F.

claim: A subset of neurons showed peak firing at the falling phase of P-waves.
source: A subset of neurons showed peak firing at the falling phase of P-waves.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the peri-event time histograms shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: This tendency was consistent between NREM and REM sleep with respect to neural firing within the brainstem, suggesting that P-waves during NREM sleep (P-wavesNREM) are equivalent to P-waves during REM sleep (P-wavesREM).
source: This tendency was consistent between NREM and REM sleep with respect to neural firing within the brainstem, suggesting that P-waves during NREM sleep (P-wavesNREM) are equivalent to P-waves during REM sleep (P-wavesREM).
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity in neural firing patterns shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: During NREM sleep, P-waves were associated with multiple oscillatory components.
source: During NREM sleep, P-waves were associated with multiple oscillatory components.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the averaged P-wave-triggered cortical EEGs shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Averaged P-wave-triggered cortical EEGs exhibited multiple phasic components, which consisted of delta (1–4 Hz), theta (~7 Hz) and beta (15 ~ 30 Hz) frequencies.
source: Averaged P-wave-triggered cortical EEGs exhibited multiple phasic components (Figure 6B), which consisted of delta (1–4 Hz), theta (~7 Hz) and beta (15 ~ 30 Hz) frequencies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spectral analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Significant phase preferences of P-wave timing were found (p<0.01, Rayleigh test).
source: We found significant phase preferences of P-wave timing (p<0.01, Rayleigh test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phase analysis shown in Figure 6C with statistical testing.

claim: Larger phase modulation was found at delta and beta ranges during NREM sleep.
source: We found larger phase modulation at delta and beta ranges.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the resultant vector length analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: P-wavesREM exhibited significant phase modulation at theta range (p<0.01).
source: We observed significant phase modulation at theta range (p<0.01) (Figure 6C), indicating that two prominent neural markers in REM sleep, that is, theta oscillations and P-waves, are temporally organized.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phase analysis shown in Figure 6C with statistical testing.

claim: Two prominent neural markers in REM sleep, that is, theta oscillations and P-waves, are temporally organized.
source: We observed significant phase modulation at theta range (p<0.01) (Figure 6C), indicating that two prominent neural markers in REM sleep, that is, theta oscillations and P-waves, are temporally organized.
evidence: This is inferred from the significant phase modulation shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The effect of sleep states on these phase-locking activities was statistically significant (F1,179 = 4.90, p<0.05, two-way ANOVA).
source: We found that the effect of sleep states on these phase-locking activities was statistically significant (F1,179 = 4.90, p<0.05, two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of phase-locking data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The temporal coupling between P-waves and cortical oscillations was modified by sleep states.
source: Hence, the temporal coupling between P-waves and cortical oscillations was modified by sleep states.
evidence: This is concluded from the state-dependent differences in phase-locking shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: The effect of sleep states on the resultant vector length was significant (F1,79 = 4.00, p<0.05, two-way ANOVA) for hippocampal LFPs.
source: We found that the effect of sleep states on the resultant vector length was significant (F1,79 = 4.00, p<0.05, two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of hippocampal LFP phase-locking shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The timing of P-waves was strongly phase-locked at the theta range (~7 Hz) in both sleep states.
source: We found that the effect of sleep states on the resultant vector length was significant (F1,79 = 4.00, p<0.05, two-way ANOVA). The timing of P-waves was strongly phase-locked at the theta range (~7 Hz) in both sleep states and there was no significant difference in the resultant vector length across frequencies, but we observed stronger phase modulations in high frequency (≥30 Hz) components during REM sleep based on the effect size.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phase analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Stronger phase modulations in high frequency (≥30 Hz) components were observed during REM sleep based on the effect size.
source: we observed stronger phase modulations in high frequency (≥30 Hz) components during REM sleep based on the effect size.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the effect size analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A subset of CA1 neurons fired most strongly around the timing of P-waves during both NREM and REM sleep.
source: Intriguingly, although a subset of CA1 neurons fired most strongly around the timing of P-waves during both NREM and REM sleep, the temporal order between CA1 neural firing and P-waves was state-dependent (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the peri-event time histograms shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The temporal order between CA1 neural firing and P-waves was state-dependent.
source: Intriguingly, although a subset of CA1 neurons fired most strongly around the timing of P-waves during both NREM and REM sleep, the temporal order between CA1 neural firing and P-waves was state-dependent (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the peri-event time histograms shown in Figure 7C.

claim: During NREM sleep, co-firing of hippocampal neurons was followed by P-waves.
source: during NREM sleep, co-firing of hippocampal neurons was followed by P-waves, whereas P-waves were followed by burst firing in a subset of CA1 neurons during REM sleep.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the peri-event time histograms shown in Figure 7C.

claim: P-waves were followed by burst firing in a subset of CA1 neurons during REM sleep.
source: during NREM sleep, co-firing of hippocampal neurons was followed by P-waves, whereas P-waves were followed by burst firing in a subset of CA1 neurons during REM sleep.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the peri-event time histograms shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Ripple events preceded P-waves during NREM sleep across all of four recordings (p<0.05, t-test).
source: We found that ripple events preceded P-waves during NREM sleep across all of four recordings (Figure 7D inset) (p<0.05, t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the temporal analysis shown in Figure 7D with statistical testing.

claim: P-waves are strongly associated with hippocampal activity in both sleep states.
source: Thus, P-waves are strongly associated with hippocampal activity in both sleep states.
evidence: This is concluded from the analyses shown in Figure 7.

claim: These associations are state-dependent.
source: However, these associations are state-dependent.
evidence: This is concluded from the state-dependent differences in temporal relationships shown in Figure 7.

claim: Brainstem neurons show diverse state-dependent firing, with cell-type-specificity in pontine cholinergic neurons.
source: On a timescale of seconds to minutes, brainstem neurons show diverse state-dependent firing, with cell-type-specificity in pontine cholinergic neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the electrophysiology and fiber photometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Brainstem activity can collectively predict pupil dilation as well as behavioral states.
source: Brainstem activity can collectively predict pupil dilation as well as behavioral states.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analyses shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The ability to predict behavioral states is longer lasting than that of hippocampal neurons.
source: The ability to predict behavioral states is longer lasting than that of hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: These relatively slow dynamics may be related to observations from optogenetic experiments in which the effect of optogenetic stimulation on state transitions often emerges tens of seconds after stimulus onset.
source: These relatively slow dynamics may be related to observations from optogenetic experiments in which the effect of optogenetic stimulation on state transitions often emerges tens of seconds after stimulus onset (Adamantidis et al., 2007; Van Dort et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2019; Tsunematsu et al., 2013; Tsunematsu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative connection to prior optogenetic studies, supported by citations.

claim: P-waves typically appear during REM sleep and less often during NREM sleep.
source: P-waves typically appear during REM sleep and less often during NREM sleep.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the frequency analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: P-waves in both sleep states are accompanied by synchronous firing of brainstem neurons, suggesting that underlying local activity during P-waves is similar between sleep states.
source: P-waves in both sleep states are accompanied by synchronous firing of brainstem neurons, suggesting that underlying local activity during P-waves is similar between sleep states.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar firing patterns shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: The relationship of P-waves to cortical neural events is state-dependent.
source: However, the relationship of P-waves to cortical neural events is state-dependent
evidence: This is demonstrated by the state-dependent differences shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The timing of P-wavesNREM are phase-locked to various cortical oscillations.
source: the timing of P-wavesNREM are phase-locked to various cortical oscillations
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phase analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: P-wavesNREM are part of the brain-wide neural events triggered by SWRs.
source: hippocampal SWRs precede P-wavesNREM, suggesting that P-wavesNREM are part of the brain-wide neural events triggered by SWRs.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal relationship shown in Figure 7D.

claim: P-waves are phase-locked most strongly at theta frequency in both the neocortex and hippocampus during REM sleep.
source: During REM sleep, P-waves are phase-locked most strongly at theta frequency in both the neocortex and hippocampus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phase analysis shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: P-waves precede firing in a subset of hippocampal CA1 neurons during REM sleep.
source: Crucially, P-waves precede firing in a subset of hippocampal CA1 neurons, suggesting that P-wavesREM may trigger brain-wide neural events.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the peri-event time histograms shown in Figure 7C.

claim: P-wavesREM may trigger brain-wide neural events.
source: Crucially, P-waves precede firing in a subset of hippocampal CA1 neurons, suggesting that P-wavesREM may trigger brain-wide neural events.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the temporal relationship shown in Figure 7C.

claim: P-waves are part of the state-dependent coordinated activity across the brain.
source: Thus, P-waves are part of the state-dependent coordinated activity across the brain.
evidence: This is concluded from the state-dependent interactions shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Silicon probe recording allowed quantification of the state dependency of brainstem neural ensemble dynamics on a timescale of seconds to minutes.
source: This approach allowed us (1) to quantify the state dependency of brainstem neural ensemble dynamics on a timescale of seconds to minutes
evidence: This is a methodological claim about what the silicon probe approach enabled.

claim: Silicon probe recording allowed decoding of vigilance states on the basis of population activity.
source: (2) to decode vigilance states on the basis of population activity
evidence: This is a methodological claim about what the silicon probe approach enabled.

claim: Silicon probe recording allowed characterization of neural population activity underlying P-waves for the first time.
source: and (3) to characterize neural population activity underlying P-waves for the first time.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about what the silicon probe approach enabled.

claim: The asymmetric profile of the predictability of pupil diameter suggests that the modulation of brainstem activity precedes pupil dilation, rather than being simply correlated to it.
source: Crucially, the asymmetric profile of the predictability of pupil diameter suggests that the modulation of brainstem activity precedes pupil dilation, rather than being simply correlated to it.
evidence: This is an inference based on the asymmetric predictability profiles shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: The long-lasting predictability of brainstem populations for behavioral states is not trivial.
source: The long-lasting predictability of brainstem populations for behavioral states is not trivial.
evidence: This is a statement emphasizing the significance of the finding.

claim: The slow (30–60 s) timescale recalls the timescale observed in some optogenetic experiments.
source: Intriguingly, the slow (30–60 s) timescale recalls us the timescale observed in some of optogenetic experiments
evidence: This is a comparison to prior optogenetic studies.

claim: Although optogenetic stimulation can modulate neural firing at a millisecond resolution, the effect of optical stimulation on state transitions typically emerges tens of seconds after stimulus onset.
source: although optogenetic stimulation can modulate neural firing at a millisecond resolution, the effect of optical stimulation on state transitions typically emerges tens of seconds after stimulus onset (Adamantidis et al., 2007; Van Dort et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior optogenetic studies.

claim: The modulation of neural activity in the brainstem occurs tens of seconds before global brain state transitions from one state to another.
source: The exact mechanism is still unknown, but we hypothesize that the modulation of neural activity in the brainstem occurs tens of seconds before global brain state transitions from one state to another.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Each state emerges from complex interactions across various regions of the brain.
source: In other words, each state emerges from complex interactions across various regions of the brain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the nature of brain state transitions.

claim: The confirmation of P-waves in mice is important for further interrogation with respect to the generation mechanism and function of P-waves.
source: Given the growing importance of mice as an animal model for sleep research (Héricé et al., 2019), the confirmation of P-waves in mice is important for further interrogation with respect to the generation mechanism and function of P-waves.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of confirming P-waves in mice.

claim: The waveform of P-waves in mice is generally consistent with those in other species, such as cats and rats.
source: First, the waveform of P-waves in mice is generally consistent with those in other species, such as cats (Callaway et al., 1987; Jeannerod et al., 1965) and rats (Datta, 1997; Farber et al., 1980), suggesting that underlying neural ensembles may be similar across species.
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior studies in other species, supported by citations.

claim: Underlying neural ensembles may be similar across species.
source: First, the waveform of P-waves in mice is generally consistent with those in other species, such as cats (Callaway et al., 1987; Jeannerod et al., 1965) and rats (Datta, 1997; Farber et al., 1980), suggesting that underlying neural ensembles may be similar across species.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the similarity of P-wave waveforms across species.

claim: The phasic firing just before (<25 ms before) the trough of P-waves resembles the observations in cats.
source: Indeed, the phasic firing just before (<25 ms before) the trough of P-waves (Figure 5) resembles the observations in cats (McCarley et al., 1978; Steriade et al., 1990; Sakai and Jouvet, 1980; Nelson et al., 1983).
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior studies in cats, supported by citations.

claim: The frequency of P-waves during REM sleep is generally consistent across species.
source: Second, the frequency of P-waves during REM sleep is generally consistent across species (Datta, 1997).
